about: The command builder's wizard, maintained by hand: the questions it asks, the options each answer offers, the sentences of 'What this command will do', and the checks that depend on the kind of file (kind_rules: refused by the CLI; kind_cautions: gates the CLI accepts but can only ever fail with exit 1). Every option it offers must exist in options.json and have a summary line that refers to it; the gates must be the CLI's --fail-on values; the services must be every host the code calls; lockfile_names must be inputs.LOCKFILES; each kind rule's args must be refused by the CLI with its message and its ok_args must not be (tests/test_builder.py checks all of these). Conditions use the rules.json operators, plus {"what": [...]}, true when the kind of input is one of those: the wizard's first answer, corrected by the file name (wizard.js kindOf), so also "renv". Text puts an option's value where {dest} is written; {malware} reads ' and malware' when OSV is used. For the paste box: ecosystems maps the names --package accepts before the colon to their purl types (inputs.ECOSYSTEMS), and version_not_allowed is the CLI's rule for what is not one version (inputs._NOT_A_VERSION, matched ignoring case).

targets.label: A project's dependency list
targets.hint: A lockfile such as package-lock.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml, go.sum or Cargo.lock: for example an npm project, or a VS Code extension's source.

targets.label: A container image
targets.hint: An image with a tag or digest, such as nginx:1.27. The scanners read it from Docker or another local runtime, or pull it from the registry.

targets.label: A file or folder you downloaded or built
targets.hint: A JAR or WAR, a wheel, an npm .tgz, a binary, or a folder of built files.

targets.label: A VS Code extension
targets.hint: A .vsix file, an installed extension's folder, or all your installed extensions (~/.vscode/extensions). Cursor and VSCodium keep theirs in ~/.cursor/extensions and ~/.vscode-oss/extensions.

targets.label: An SBOM or a package list
targets.hint: A CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM, a folder of them, or a .csv with ecosystem,name,version (or purl) columns.

targets.label: Specific packages
targets.hint: One or more packages by name and version, such as npm:chalk@5.6.1. Nothing to download first.

targets.label: Just a GitHub project's health
targets.hint: Releases, OpenSSF Scorecard and GitHub Actions workflows, without checking any packages.

path.label: Where is it?
path.hint: The path on your computer. ~/ means your home folder.

image.label: Which image?
image.hint: Name and an explicit tag or digest, such as owner/app:1.2.3.

image_src.label: Where should the scanners read it from?
image_src.hint: Leave it to the scanners unless you know: 'remote' pulls from the registry without Docker.

package.label: Which packages?
package.hint: ecosystem:name@version, or a purl such as pkg:pypi/django@2.2.0. One per row.

label.label: Labels (optional)
label.hint: Group the results, such as owner=Web team. One per row.

repo.label: Where is the source on GitHub?
repo.hint: owner/name. Optional for everything but a project check: it adds release cadence, Scorecard and the workflow audit.

out.label: Folder for the report
out.hint: Created if it does not exist.

fail_on_likelihood.label: Also fail if the suggested likelihood is at least
fail_on_likelihood.hint: A 1 to 5 heuristic from the findings and the project's signals. Leave it unset for no likelihood gate.

outcomes.label: A report to read
outcomes.hint: Exits 0 whenever the run completes, whatever it finds.

outcomes.label: A pass or fail check, for CI
outcomes.hint: Exits 3 when something you pick below is found, and 1 if a check it needs could not run.

gates.label: A package is known malware
gates.summary: a package known to be malware

gates.label: A vulnerability is known to be exploited (CISA KEV)
gates.summary: a vulnerability in CISA's known-exploited list

gates.label: Anything in Act now: malware, exploited, or a ready-made exploit
gates.summary: a finding in the Act now group (malware, exploited, or a ready-made exploit)

gates.label: A package version published in the last few days
gates.summary: a package version published in the last {release_age_days} days

gates.label: A package version whose release date can't be found
gates.summary: a package version whose release date could not be found

gates.label: The file doesn't match the checksum its registry publishes (JAR, wheel, sdist or npm .tgz)
gates.summary: a file that does not match its registry checksum

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: the dependency list {path} for known vulnerabilities{malware}, with {scanners}. It reads the file; nothing is installed or run.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: the container image {image} for known vulnerabilities{malware}, with {scanners}.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: The image is pulled from the registry, without Docker.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: The scanners read the image from {image_src}.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: {path} for known vulnerabilities{malware}, with {scanners}.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: A JAR, wheel, sdist or npm .tgz is also compared with the checksum its registry (Maven Central, PyPI or npm) publishes for that version.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: the VS Code extension {path}: whether the VS Code Marketplace removed it and why, what its own files show it can do (starting with VS Code, starting programs, native code, hidden characters, encoded strings), and the npm packages it ships, for known vulnerabilities{malware}, with {scanners}. A .vsix is unpacked with limits; nothing in it is installed or run.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: every package listed in {path} against OSV, for known vulnerabilities and malware. No scanner is needed.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: the CRAN packages in the R renv.lock {path} against OSV, for known vulnerabilities and malware; packages from Bioconductor, GitHub or local sources are not checked. No scanner is needed.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: {path}: a lockfile, file or folder with {scanners}, or an SBOM or .csv package list against OSV.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: {package} against OSV, for known vulnerabilities and malware. No scanner is needed.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: only the GitHub project {repo}: no packages are checked.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: Malware is seen only in advisories Trivy or Grype class as malicious, since OSV's malware data is not queried.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: Uses the Trivy report in {from_trivy_json} instead of running Trivy.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: Uses the Grype report in {from_grype_json} instead of running Grype.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: Labels each package with {label}, where it has no such label yet.

summary.head: Checks
summary.text: Leaves out findings below {min_severity}.

summary.head: Also checks
summary.text: {repo} on GitHub: its releases and how often it makes them.

summary.head: Also checks
summary.text: its release dates, to tell whether fixes were out before the release.

summary.head: Also checks
summary.text: its OpenSSF Scorecard.

summary.head: Also checks
summary.text: its GitHub Actions workflows, for unpinned and known-bad actions.

summary.head: Also checks
summary.text: each vulnerability it finds for signs of exploitation (CISA KEV, FIRST EPSS and public exploit indexes), to suggest what to fix first.

summary.head: Also checks
summary.text: when each fix was published, to measure how long fixes have been available.

summary.head: Also checks
summary.text: Go binaries with govulncheck: is the vulnerable function in the binary?

summary.head: Also checks
summary.text: Carries your earlier decisions forward from {decisions}.

summary.head: Flags
summary.text: any language package version (npm, PyPI, Maven, Go and the others deps.dev covers) published in the last {release_age_days} days; OS packages are not checked. New releases are when compromised versions are live, before advisories catch up.

summary.head: Flags
summary.text: a suggested likelihood from 1 to 5, built from the findings and the project's signals. It is a starting point for an assessor, not a risk rating.

summary.head: Fails
summary.text: with exit code 3 if it finds {fail_on}.

summary.head: Fails
summary.text: with exit code 3 if the suggested likelihood is {fail_on_likelihood} or higher.

summary.head: Fails
summary.text: with exit code 1, rather than passing, if a check one of these gates needs could not run and no gate was tripped.

summary.head: Fails
summary.text: The checksum gate compares a JAR, wheel, sdist or npm .tgz with the checksum its registry publishes for that version. When it cannot (a binary, a JAR without its Maven details, a version the registry does not have, or a failed lookup), the gate exits 1 rather than passing. A folder, lockfile or package list is refused before the run starts.

summary.head: Fails
summary.text: never on what it finds: it exits 0 when the run completes. For CI, add a pass or fail check.

summary.head: Writes
summary.text: {formats} to {out}.

summary.head: Writes
summary.text: The scanners' own output goes in {out}/raw.

summary.head: Writes
summary.text: packages.csv too, one row per package.

summary.head: Writes
summary.text: a CycloneDX SBOM from Trivy, in {out}/raw.

summary.head: Writes
summary.text: Prints only errors and the final summary.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: anything that needs the network (offline): OSV, release dates, exploitation signals and the GitHub project. A zero for these means not checked, not clean.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: {repo}: offline skips GitHub.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: the project's health: add where its source is on GitHub.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: the project's own code, or whether what you install (for example a .vsix from the VS Code Marketplace) was built from this source: only the listed dependencies are checked.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: how new each package version is, or when fixes were published: R packages are not looked up on deps.dev.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: anything the SBOM or package list leaves out: only the packages it names are checked.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: that the scanners on your computer are the genuine releases: pin their versions and hashes under All options.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: whether the vulnerable code is reachable where you run it: a finding is a version match, not proof of exposure.

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: CISA KEV (turned off).

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: FIRST EPSS (turned off).

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: public exploit indexes (turned off).

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: the OpenSSF Scorecard (turned off).

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: the project's GitHub Actions workflows (turned off).

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: when fixes were published (turned off).

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: the registry checksum (turned off).

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: how new each package version is (turned off).

summary.head: Doesn't check
summary.text: whether what an indicator shows is harmful: an extension runs with your rights, so read each one against what the extension is for. Nor the Marketplace signature, or the code of a bundled extension's dependencies.

services.sends: the file's package name and version

Fix-date records (Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat, Alpine, Packagist and Go)

scanner_notes.text: Trivy and Grype download their vulnerability databases from their own servers, unless their copy is fresh.
The scanners pull the image from its registry if it is not on your computer (always, with remote), with your registry login if Docker has one.
For a pom.xml, Trivy fetches the parent and dependency POMs from Maven Central and from any repository the pom.xml or your Maven settings name.
govulncheck downloads the Go vulnerability database from vuln.go.dev; for an image, Docker or crane pulls the image to copy its binaries out.

privacy_notes.text: Your files are read on your computer. Apart from what the scanners fetch, only the names and IDs listed are sent.
The file is read on your computer: only the names and IDs listed are sent.

kind_rules.message: osv needs the package list from trivy
--label applies to a package inventory or SBOM, or to --package
--fail-on mismatch needs a single file to compare with its registry

kind_cautions.message: --fail-on recent and unknown-age cannot be checked for renv.lock (R packages' release dates are not looked up), so the run would always exit 1
